verses.translation_literal: A psalm, a song for the day of the Sabbath.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm. A song, set apart for the Sabbath day.
verses.directors_commentary: This title is the only heading in the Psalter that names a day of the week, and the Hebrew counts it as verse 1, which is why every verse here is one higher than in the KJV. The tradition behind the Mishnah's list of daily psalms took it as the song for the Sabbath, sung in the Temple. Rashi says it was recited on Sabbaths and speaks of the world to come, a world that is wholly Sabbath; Metzudat David says it was set to be sung from the platform in the Temple. The Targum goes further and has Adam say it. Keep that range in mind: the day itself, rest from work, is the stage on which everything after this is sung. The KJV's 'Psalm or Song' is fine, but the two Hebrew words are joined as a pair, a psalm with instruments and a song with voice, and the listener should hear both.

philological_notes.note: A psalm, a piece sung to the accompaniment of strings or plucked instruments; the root is the same as the verb 'to sing praises' in verse 2, so the title sounds the theme of the opening line.

'For the day of the Sabbath'. Rashi on Psalms 92:1 says it was said on Sabbaths and speaks of the world to come, which is entirely Sabbath; Radak on Psalms 92:1 says it was said in the Temple on the Sabbath.

verses.translation_literal: Good [it is] to give thanks to YHWH, and to sing praises to your name, O Most High,
verses.translation_dramatic: It is good to give thanks to the LORD, good to make music to your name, O Most High.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with a single flat word, 'good', and holds it before the infinitives arrive. The speaker is not asking permission or setting a mood; the Sabbath is the one day on which this is the only job. Radak says the day is better than the other days because a man is free of the business of the world. The KJV's 'It is a good thing' adds a word the Hebrew does not have: the Hebrew simply says 'Good', and then shows what is good. Hebrew 'to give thanks' (from ידה) is also 'to confess, to acknowledge' aloud, so the first verb is a public statement, not private feeling. 'Most High', Elyon, is an old title that Israel shares with the surrounding peoples and uses of YHWH alone; Malbim says the name is known even among the nations. The vocative at the end of the verse arrives late, as if the singer turns his face up only after the praise has begun.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil infinitive: 'to give thanks, to acknowledge'. The root carries both thanks and open confession of who someone is, so this is a public act.
'Most High', a title of God as the highest above all. Malbim on Psalms 92:2 says that under this name God became known among the nations as the God of gods.

verses.translation_literal: To declare in the morning your steadfast love, and your faithfulness in the nights.
verses.translation_dramatic: To tell it at the break of morning: your steadfast love. And through the long nights: your faithfulness.
verses.directors_commentary: Two times and two words are laid out as a pair: morning with chesed, nights with emunah. Chesed is loyal love that keeps a bond when it has no duty to; emunah is steadiness, that which can be leaned on. The KJV's 'lovingkindness' is a Coverdale coinage that makes chesed sound like soft feeling, and 'every night' flattens the Hebrew plural 'in the nights'. The nights are many, and they may be hard ones. Rashi hears exile in them: in the night of the exile one keeps faith that God will keep his promise, and in the morning of redemption one declares his love. Radak, on the other hand, reads the Sabbath eve and the night after it as nights of rest. The text allows both: morning is easy to praise, night is where faithfulness has to be believed. A reader should feel the long breath in the second half, which has no verb of its own and borrows 'to declare' from the first.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love; paired here with emunah as the two faces of God's reliability. Malbim on Psalms 92:3 distinguishes chesed as the miraculous governing of the world and emunah as the fixed order of nature.
A plural: 'in the nights', not 'every night'. Rashi on Psalms 92:3 reads the nights as the time of the exile; Radak on Psalms 92:3 as the nights of Sabbath rest.

verses.translation_literal: On a ten-stringed [instrument], and on a harp, on a murmur with a lyre.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the ten-stringed instrument and on the harp, with the soft murmur of the lyre beneath it.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a verse of instruments, and the actors should let the strings sound. The 'ten' is a ten-stringed instrument (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David); the nevel is the harp, the large, deep-voiced instrument, and the kinnor is the lyre, the handheld one that David is remembered for. The KJV's instruments are right in number, but its names are old: 'psaltery' is a harp, and its 'harp' for kinnor is really a lyre. Its 'with a solemn sound' is a guess, and it hangs the phrase on the harp. The BBE collapses the whole verse to 'an instrument of music with a quiet sound'. The odd word is higgayon, which lies between humming, murmured thought and spoken meditation; the same root is used for the blessed man who 'meditates' on the Torah in Psalm 1. Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as the pleasantness of the melody, Metzudat David as a spoken song that the lyre smooths. After the morning and the night of verse 3, the psalm now supplies an orchestra. In the Temple the singing was the work of the Levite singers; here the instruments stand for the whole sound of the congregation's praise.

philological_notes.note: 'A ten': an instrument of ten strings. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David all say so; the Hebrew has only the number.
From the root for murmuring, muttering, meditating. Radak on Psalms 92:4 takes it as the sweetness of the song said over the lyre; Metzudat Zion on Psalms 92:4 defines it simply as speech.

verses.translation_literal: For you have made me glad, YHWH, by your deed; in the works of your hands I shout for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you have made me glad, LORD, in what you have done; in the work of your hands I cry out for joy.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason for the praise arrives with 'for': the singer is not obliged to sing, he is glad. The verse is built as a mirror, 'your deed' against 'the works of your hands', and the Hebrew shows two different words for what God does: pa'al is the doing, the act, and ma'aseh is the finished work. Malbim sees the difference in just that way, a doing still under hand against a work completed. The KJV's 'triumph' for the verb is a stretch: ranan is the ringing cry of joy, a loud shout, closer to singing out loud than to winning. 'The works of your hands' is the language of a craftsman and shows God as a potter, a builder. Radak says the gladness comes on the Sabbath, from having leisure to think over the world; Metzudat David reads it as the saving acts done for the singer. The shift from perfect ('you have made me glad') to imperfect ('I will cry out') takes the singer from what happened to what he now cannot stop doing.

philological_notes.note: 'By your deed, your doing'. Malbim on Psalms 92:5 says pa'al is the ongoing activity, ma'aseh the completed work.
'I shout for joy': a ringing cry, not a quiet hymn and not a victory ('triumph' in the KJV).

verses.translation_literal: How great are your works, YHWH! Exceedingly deep are your thoughts.
verses.translation_dramatic: How great, LORD, are your works! And how very deep your thoughts.
verses.directors_commentary: An exclamation: mah, 'how!', is a gasp, not a question. Greatness is measured upward and depth downward, and Ibn Ezra notes that 'great' and 'high' are the same direction, while 'deep' is the opposite, 'and all of it against a man'. God's works are visible and large; his thoughts, his plans and purposes, are hidden and far down. That sets up the problem the next verses take up: why do the wicked do well? Radak puts the question as: why did God create the world when he did and not earlier? Malbim says the works are the ordered nature all can see, and the thoughts the hidden governing that the wicked and the fool fail to understand. The KJV's 'and' before the second half is not in the Hebrew; the two halves are set side by side, with no connective, and the actor should leave the pause. The adverb 'exceedingly' sits in front of the verb it modifies, leaning on 'deep'.

philological_notes.note: 'Your thoughts, plans, purposes'. Metzudat David on Psalms 92:6 says these are deep things that cannot be understood.

verses.translation_literal: A brutish man does not know, and a fool does not understand this.
verses.translation_dramatic: The brute does not know it. The fool will not grasp this.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is two lines saying the same thing with two verbs and two kinds of people, and Ibn Ezra says the sense is doubled. 'Brutish' (ba'ar) is the language of cattle: the root is the one for livestock, and Metzudat Zion ties it to the word for 'our beasts' in Numbers 20. A ba'ar is a man who thinks like an animal, who sees grass and sees only grass. The KJV's 'brutish' catches this; the BBE's 'a man without sense' loses it. 'Fool' (kesil) is the thick, dull, self-satisfied one of Proverbs. 'Know' and 'understand' are different: yada is to perceive, bin is to discern. 'This' points ahead to the next verse, as Rashi and Metzudat David both say: the thing that does not get understood is that the flourishing of the wicked is the road to their ruin. Delivery is flat and almost bored, and the contempt lies in the plain verbs.

philological_notes.note: 'Brutish, stupid like a beast'. Metzudat Zion on Psalms 92:7 ties it to the word for beasts in Numbers 20.
'This': points forward to the next verse. Rashi on Psalms 92:7 says it is what is said below; Metzudat David on Psalms 92:7 agrees.

verses.translation_literal: When the wicked sprout like grass, and all the doers of iniquity blossom, [it is] that they be destroyed until ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked spring up like grass; every worker of mischief bursts into flower. And all of it only so that they may be swept away, forever.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the solution to the riddle of the last two verses, and it is cruel. The wicked flourish, but the image is chosen with care: eshev is the fast-growing green of a wet season, the grass of the field that is up in days and gone in the first heat. Radak says just that: success comes fast and the grass withers fast, while for the righteous the psalm will use the palm and the cedar. 'Sprout' and 'blossom' are the same pair as in a garden; the actors can play the sneer of the onlooker who sees only the bloom. The last clause is the hinge. The KJV's 'it is that they shall be destroyed' is a very loose bridge, and the Hebrew has a bare infinitive with 'to', 'to be destroyed', and then 'until ever, until forever', with 'adei 'ad' sounding the same word twice. Rashi cites Deuteronomy 7:10 (God repays those who hate him to their face, to destroy them): the success is a payment in advance. Radak and Metzudat David read it that way, as a small reward in this world for a few good deeds, which then makes the loss in the next world complete. 'Iniquity' (aven) is wickedness with a hint of emptiness and trouble.

philological_notes.note: Green plants, herbage, grass. Radak on Psalms 92:8 notes it flourishes fast and dries as fast, in contrast to the palm and cedar said of the righteous.
Niphal infinitive with a pronoun: 'for their being destroyed', a purpose or outcome clause. Rashi on Psalms 92:8 cites Deuteronomy 7:10 and reads it as God's purpose in letting them flourish.

verses.translation_literal: And you, height, for ever, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD, are on high. Forever.
verses.directors_commentary: At the center of a psalm of sixteen verses sits a verse of four words, with no verb. The Hebrew says 'And you, height'. It does not say 'most high', as the KJV has it, nor 'art', which is supplied; the noun marom is a place, 'the height'. God is not described as being high, he is the height. Everything before the verse is the ground-level view of the flourishing of the wicked, and everything after depends on this one. Rashi says that in all of God's judgments his hand is on the upper side, so all declare his verdict just; Radak says that even when the wicked succeed no one should say there is no one watching: there is, and the time will come. Malbim adds a point about power: a human king may fail to punish rebels because they are out of reach or because he may die, but God is high and for ever. The actors should drop the volume here, not raise it. The name YHWH comes last, and it lands on the word 'for ever' like a seal.

philological_notes.note: 'Height': a noun, not an adjective. The Hebrew has no verb. Rashi on Psalms 92:9 reads it as God's hand always being on the upper side in judgment; Radak on Psalms 92:9 as God seeing all.

verses.translation_literal: For behold your enemies, YHWH, for behold your enemies, they will perish; they will be scattered, all the doers of iniquity.
verses.translation_dramatic: For look: your enemies, LORD. Look: your enemies will perish. They will be scattered, every one who works iniquity.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse begins twice. 'For behold your enemies, YHWH' is stopped before it finishes, and the singer starts again with the same words, and this time the verb comes. It is an old device of Hebrew song, and Radak says the repetition is for strength. The KJV keeps the repetition, which is correct, but the BBE removes it and in doing so loses the stammer. The effect is of a man pointing, 'Look!', and needing a moment before he can say what he sees. The repeated 'your enemies' also reminds us whose enemies they are: not the singer's, but God's, and the fate they will meet follows from that. 'Perish' and 'scatter' are an unmatched pair, destruction and dispersal: Malbim says they may break apart of themselves, because evil work cannot hold together. The Hebrew of the second verb is reflexive in form, which is why YLT says 'separate themselves'. The word 'iniquity' returns from verse 8 and ties the two verses together: the workers of iniquity who bloomed are the ones who now come apart.

philological_notes.note: 'Behold, look!': a pointing word. It is doubled here with the whole phrase 'your enemies'; Radak on Psalms 92:10 says the repetition is for emphasis.
Hithpael of 'to separate': 'they will be scattered' or 'they will separate themselves'. Malbim on Psalms 92:10 takes it as falling apart of their own accord.

verses.translation_literal: And you raise my horn like the wild ox; I am drenched in fresh oil.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you lift up my horn like the horn of the wild ox. Fresh oil is poured over me, and I am soaked in it.
verses.directors_commentary: The first word mirrors verse 9. 'You are height' (marom) turns into 'you raised up' (tarem), from the same root: because God is on high, he lifts. Ibn Ezra says so. The 'horn' is strength and dignity; a raised horn is a head held high. The re'em is the wild ox, the aurochs, a huge animal of the Near East that was already extinct in much of the world by the Middle Ages, and the KJV's 'unicorn' is a famous error that comes from the Greek and Latin monokeros, 'one-horned', although the Hebrew animal had two. The ASV and YLT correct to 'wild ox' and 'reem'. The second half is harder. Baloti, 'I have been mixed, soaked', is from a verb meaning to mix flour with oil, as in Numbers 15:9, which Rashi cites. The picture is not a drop on the head but a head wet through with fresh, green oil. Radak reads ra'anan as moist and rich, a sign of abundance; fresh oil is a mark of status and festivity, like the anointing of kings and guests. The speaker is a single figure, but Radak says the poet speaks for every righteous person.

philological_notes.note: 'Like a wild ox' (the aurochs, Bos primigenius). The KJV's 'unicorn' follows the Greek monokeros. Metzudat Zion on Psalms 92:11 simply names it an animal, the re'em.
From בלל, 'to mix, to moisten'. Rashi on Psalms 92:11 compares Numbers 15:9, 'mixed with oil'; Radak on Psalms 92:11 allows that it may be passive or may mean 'I [have anointed] my head'.

verses.translation_literal: And my eye has looked on my watchful foes; on those who rise up against me, evildoers, my ears hear.
verses.translation_dramatic: My eye has looked on those who watched me with hate. And of the evildoers who rose against me, my ears have heard.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm closes its first half with the eye and the ear, the two senses of witness. The Hebrew is spare: the eye 'looks', the ears 'hear', and the verse says no more about what is seen or heard. The KJV adds 'my desire' twice, in italics, to make a sentence, and the added words tilt the whole verse towards revenge; ASV keeps them too. YLT, which does not add them, is closer. Radak and Metzudat David do read it as what the singer longed to see, but that is their reading of the silence, not the Hebrew. The first noun, shurai, is rare: the root means to watch, to gaze at, and Metzudat Zion points to the clause 'I behold him, but not near' (אֲשׁוּרֶנּוּ וְלֹא קָרוֹב, Numbers 24:17), so these are enemies who watch and wait for a fall, 'my watchers' in a hostile sense. Rashi and Ibn Ezra link it to a more familiar word for foes in Psalm 5:9. Rashi, citing the Talmud, imagines the singer hearing from behind the heavenly curtain that the plot will not succeed. The effect is of a man who stood in the dark while others plotted, and now stands in the open and sees and hears the result.

philological_notes.note: 'On those who watch me': from שור 'to gaze, to look hostilely'. Rashi on Psalms 92:12 and Ibn Ezra on Psalms 92:12 connect it to the word for foes in Psalm 5:9; Metzudat Zion on Psalms 92:12 ties it to the verb of 'I behold him, but not near' (אֲשׁוּרֶנּוּ וְלֹא קָרוֹב, Numbers 24:17).
Hiphil participle: 'those who do evil'; sits in apposition after 'those who rise up against me', so the rebels are defined by their conduct.

verses.translation_literal: [The] righteous [one], like the palm, will flourish; like a cedar in the Lebanon, he will grow tall.
verses.translation_dramatic: The righteous stand like the palm, and, like the palm, they burst into bloom. Like the cedar on the heights of Lebanon, they rise, and rise again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse sets two trees side by side, and the audience knows both. The palm (tamar) is the tree of the oasis and the lowland: slender, straight, green at the crown through the dry season, and heavy with dates. The cedar is the tree of the mountain, broad, dark and enormously long-lived, the timber of palaces and temples. One tree gives fruit, the other height and endurance; Rashi reads it exactly so, the palm for bearing fruit and the cedar for renewing its trunk, and Metzudat David adds that the palm's fruit is children. Play the pair as range: from the valley floor to the peak.

The KJV 'shall flourish... shall grow' is fair, but it makes the two verbs look like synonyms; the first (parach) is the opening of buds and blossoms, the second (sagah, kin to sagi', 'great') is sheer size, as Radak notes. The Hebrew also leaves the cedar without a 'like... in': 'like a cedar in the Lebanon' carries the definite article, the Lebanon, the mountain range itself, which every Israelite knew as the home of the great trees. And the KJV's 'the palm tree' is correct; BBE's 'a tall tree' erases the image. The singular 'righteous one' (tzaddiq) is a type, not a named man.

philological_notes.note: To grow great, to increase in size. The root is related to שַׂגִּיא ('great', 'abundant') and describes growth in height and bulk rather than blossoming.
The date palm. The bare noun is the tree; its fruit is not named here. The same word was a woman's name (Tamar), and a palm was a common emblem of grace and uprightness.

verses.translation_literal: Planted ones in the house of YHWH, in the courts of our God, they will flourish.
verses.translation_dramatic: Planted in the house of the LORD, rooted in the courts of our God, they come into bloom.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture changes from wild trees to a garden. The word is shatul, 'transplanted': a tree that someone has dug up and set in chosen ground, not one that grew by chance. The righteous are rooted by hand, and the soil is the temple. The KJV 'those that be planted' is archaic but accurate; it makes a clause where the Hebrew has a single bare participle, 'planted ones', which opens the verse with a jolt.

The Hebrew also separates 'house' from 'courts' with the two prepositions, and the commentators read the difference: Radak says the priests and Levites are in the house and Israel in the courts, and Metzudat David sees the doubling as emphasis. For a stage, the courts are the open ground where trees can stand and light can reach them, which suits the verb. The KJV's 'in the courts' is right; BBE's 'gardens' is an interpretation, not a translation. The last word is another form of parach: the flourishing of v.13 has now been given a place.

philological_notes.note: Passive participle of 'to plant, transplant': trees set out deliberately in a chosen place, in contrast to wild growth. Malbim stresses that a shatul is a tree uprooted from one place and planted in another.
Hiphil of 'to bloom': they cause to bloom, they put out blossom. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'bring forth a flower'. The verb in v.13 was the simple form (Qal).

verses.translation_literal: Still they will bear fruit in old age; fat and fresh they will be.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even in white-haired age they go on bearing, heavy with sap and green with leaf, as full of life as they were in spring.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse that overturns the ancient expectation. In an agrarian world, old trees and old people both dry out and stop giving; a farmer expects a worn-out vine to be cut. The Psalm says the opposite of these planted ones: 'still', od, they yield. Meiri makes the point that trees and animals reach a limit of growth, but the righteous do not.

The KJV 'fat and flourishing' is stiff. Dashen is literally 'fat', rich in oil and sap, the opposite of the dry, lean look of old age; ra'anan, 'fresh, green', is the word used for a living olive or a leafy tree (Jeremiah 17:8 shows it in the text Metzudat Zion cites). The ASV's 'full of sap and green' catches both words best. The KJV is also softer than the Hebrew in 'in old age': seivah is the grey hair itself, 'in grey-headedness'. The yield is not only children, as Malbim and the Targum read it, but also a body still able to serve. Keep the actors' voices warm and unhurried: this is a promise to the old, said in a room full of them.

philological_notes.note: Grey hair, hoary old age: the word names the white head, not just the number of years.
Fat, rich, full of sap: abundance, not obesity. Metzudat Zion and Rashi gloss it 'fat'; the image is a tree well fed with oil and moisture.

verses.translation_literal: To declare that YHWH [is] upright, my Rock, and there is no injustice in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: All of it so that it may be told: the LORD is upright. He is my Rock, and in him there is no wrong, none at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
The long picture of trees ends in a purpose: a green old age exists to be a witness. The verb is lehagid, 'to declare, tell out', which is a public act, a voice raised in the open. The commentators differ on who declares and when; Malbim has the old speak, Radak has the whole world speak in the days of the messiah, but both hear a sentence that must be said out loud, as at the end of a trial.

It is also an answer to the question that runs through the whole psalm, that the wicked sprout like grass (v.8) while the faithful suffer. The claim is theodicy: nothing crooked, in the Rock. The KJV 'to shew' is archaic for 'to declare', and 'unrighteousness' blurs avlah, which is the plain word for injustice, a bent scale. The Hebrew sets 'upright' (yashar, straight) against 'injustice' (the crooked), so the plumb-line is the picture. 'Rock' (tzur) is the psalmist's own title for God, a high, hard refuge in a land of cliffs, in the first-person form 'my Rock'. The text has a Ketiv/Qere: written without the vav, read with it; Radak and Meiri both say the sense is unchanged.

philological_notes.note: Injustice, wrong, perversion. Written without the vav (Ketiv) and read as עוֹלָתָה with it (Qere); the sense is the same, and Radak and Meiri comment on the spelling. The ending -ah is an old form of the noun.
'My rock': a cliff, a mountain fastness, and so a figure for God as a safe and unmoving place. Targum renders it 'my strength' (tqpy).
